gamespot.com/articles/get-the-entire-met.excerpt: While I’m a fan of the Stalker games, there’s something about the more linear nature and, ironically, on-rails experience that the Metro games deliver. With a tense atmosphere, mutated creatures, and factions split within the underground of a demolished Russia, the Metro series might be some of my favorite FPS games of all time—and with Metro 2039 almost here, now’s the chance to catch up on the series for less than $9. That’s all three of the games released so far. The series starts with Metro 2033 , two decades after an apocalyptic event ended most of mankind and turned the surface into a radioactive wasteland. Even breathing the air is enough to kill you, but the monstrous creatures above will do that far quicker. You play as Artyom, who leaves the safety of his home station in order to warn the rest of the metro about a new, mysterious mutant threat called the Dark Ones. I can’t really go into more detail on Metro Last Light without spoiling the predecessor. So, just take my word for it: it is arguably better, with a great narrative bolstered by gameplay improvements. Metro Exodus follows Artyom as he believes life still continues outside of Moscow, and aboard the Aurora train alongside his wife and the Spartan Rangers, he heads off to discover the truth. In all three of the Metro games, you’re limited to a first-person view, putting you face-to-face with enemies of the human and mutant variety. gamespot.com/articles/see-the-ripped-gam.title: See Ripped Game Of Thrones Actor’s Pitch To Play God Of War’s Kratos In Role Already Cast By Another Ripped Actor
gamespot.com/articles/see-the-ripped-gam.excerpt: God of War fans have been on a rollercoaster ride recently while waiting for the TV show adaptation to come to life. After originally casting Ryan Hurst for the role, Amazon was forced to find another suitably ripped actor after Hurst was horrifically injured on set. Last week his replacement, Dave Bautista, showed off his transformation so far for the role. Now, though, Game of Thrones actor Hafþór Júlíus Björnsson, or Thor Bjornsson, who played The Mountain in the HBO series, has shared an image depicting him as Kratos, asking fans if they'd like to see him take on the role. https://twitter.com/ThorBjornsson_/status/2096705259036946858?s=20 Posting on X , Bjornsson captioned the image, "Be honest... would you guys want to see me as Kratos?" The image, likely generated by AI, shows the ripped actor in an even more ripped state, dressed in Kratos' attire, complete with his trademark red tattoo, inked to honor his brother, Deimos. Of course, with Bautista already cast, Bjornsson's desire to portray Kratos is merely a wish, and isn't likely to come to fruition, but it's fun to see the towering 6 foot 9 Icelandic strongman looking like a Spartan warrior. Several other actors have expressed a desire to play the role, including Christopher Judge, the game's original voice actor. However, he's pretty frustrated that TV show adaptations regularly fail to hire anyone that worked on the source material. The God of War TV show is expected to resume production in late October or early November, although there's no estimated release date for the series just yet.

gamespot.com/articles/the-weirdest-world.title: The Weirdest Worlds That Could Technically Be In Kingdom Hearts 4
gamespot.com/articles/the-weirdest-world.excerpt: Over the past couple weeks, we've finally learned a bit more about the next entry in Square Enix's Kingdom Hearts series. In an extended Kingdom Hearts 4 trailer revealed during D23 , Disney's annual fan event, we were given a first look at Coco's Land of The Dead, and its narrative implications already have us speculating as to what worlds could come next . But while pondering what worlds could realistically be in Kingdom Hearts 4 is fun, you know what's even better? Thinking about all of the world that could technically be in Kingdom Hearts 4, with no regards to how absolutely baffling their inclusion might be. In the years since the Kingdom Hearts series first began, Disney has flexed its mouse money and purchased a lot of various companies and properties, and though you're probably well aware that Disney owns both Marvel and Star Wars, that's just scratching the surface of everything Mickey Mouse has gobbled up. Naturally, having access to all of these properties means that Disney could include them in Kingdom Hearts, so here are some of the weirdest places we could (but probably won't) go to in Sora's next adventure. Pandora (Avatar) Though I can imagine a world in which Sora joins up with Aang, Katara, and the gang, we're talking about the blue Avatar here. Sure, James Cameron still owns the creative rights to his sprawling sci-fi franchise, but Disney's merger with 20th Century Fox gave the company both distribution and merchandising rights to Avatar, as well as the ability to use the property so long as Cameron gives his permission. The ball is in your court, Jim. -- Jessica Cogswell Philadelphia (It's Always Sunny In Philadelphia) Having already crossed over with Abbott Elementary, It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia has already shown it can be brought over into a less R-rated world. gamespot.com/articles/the-best-tabletop-.title: The Best Tabletop Role-Playing Games To Play That Aren’t Dungeons & Dragons
gamespot.com/articles/the-best-tabletop-.excerpt: Tabletop role-playing games have reached an all-time high in popularity. Turns out, there’s a certain appeal about rounding up a group of friends together to go through an adventure while chucking dice in the process. For over half a century, the juggernaut of the genre has been none other than Dungeons & Dragons, designed by Gary Gygax and made super-popular through Critical Role, Stranger Things, multiple feature films, and countless other media. While the latest iteration of the fantastic game might be the best it's been in years, you're missing out if you haven't stopped to consider its alternatives. Whether you're looking for a lighter rules systems, different settings, or an entirely different concept, there has never been a better time to explore other RPG systems. Here’s a quick rundown of a few of the best out there. Mork Borg Have you ever felt that D&D was getting a bit too cozy? Maybe the sometimes-crunchy rules for combat drag down the flow of the game. Maybe you just want to roll up a complete scumbag of a character and D&D’s ruleset don’t really facilitate that. Well, Mork Borg just might be for you! A rules-lite system that owes more to the Old School Renaissance (OSR) movement of RPG design that aims to recreate rules similar to the original editions of D&D, Mork Borg puts a unique spin on setting and atmosphere. Inspired by the extreme tone of Doom Metal album covers and music, the game has players roll up a scumbag of a character with little hope of surviving in a doomed plane. I'd highly recommend it to fans of the dark fantasy genre, Darkest Dungeon, and other grim games. However, if fantasy's not your bag, give its spin-off Cy_Borg a try, as it amps up the violence and chaos of a game like Cyberpunk 2077 to 11. AMC’s The Walking Dead: The Role-Playing Game Okay, hear me out. I know the years haven’t been kind to The Walking Dead television series or its ungodly amount of spin-offs, but I found myself thoroughly impressed with this rule system.

rockpapershotgun.com/new-horror-game-the.excerpt: "Never show the monster," horror film-makers, game-makers and other creepozoids have chanted, over the decades. The Well Is Not Empty wastes no time showing us the monster - one of the monsters, at least - and doesn't seem especially the worse for it. I mean, it's the worse, but in a good way. Look, you can see the monster right there, hunkered up like a frightened puppy in the corner of the room. A scrawny little fellow with broken xylophone teeth and eyes that genuinely do make me think of the view from the bottom of a well. The monster is no threat, as long as you stay out of grabbing distance - and as long as the lights are on. The problem, as you've already guessed, is that the lights are unreliable.
